title: Why do I miss typos in my own writing? Causes and a Mac fix routine
metaTitle: Why do I miss typos in my own writing? Mac fixes that work
description: You miss typos in your own drafts because you read what you meant. Here is why it happens and free Mac fixes for Pages and Word.
targetKeyword: why do I miss typos in my own writing
secondaryKeywords: proofread your own writing on Mac
intro: You miss typos in your own writing because you read the meaning you intended, not the letters on the page. Published research backs this up. In one set of figures, people caught 59% of their own word errors after 20 minutes. This page covers why it happens, what it costs, and free Mac fixes that work in Pages and Word.
tldr: You read the meaning you meant, so your eye fills in the right word.
Real-word errors like 'affect' for 'effect' are the hardest to catch, and the figures show it.
Reading aloud, waiting before the final pass and getting a second reader all help, according to the sources here.
Pages and Word have built-in checks, but they cannot judge meaning. Read the text yourself.
Lazur can point at the right menu item, guide each click and answer out loud. It does not click for you.

blocks.text: Why your brain skips typos in your own draft

You wrote the sentence, so you already know what it says. When you reread, your eyes follow that meaning, not the letters. A typo like 'form' for 'from' looks correct because the sentence makes sense to you. The mistake and the word you intended blur into one.

Researchers have tested this directly. In 1987, Glynda Hull at UC Berkeley had skilled and less skilled college writers correct sentence-level errors. Some worked on their own essay. Others worked on three essays written by other people. Both groups corrected very few errors in their own essays, and both did better overall on the texts they did not write. BYU Editing Research summarizes the study. That summary reports no sample size and no error percentages, so read it as a pattern, not a measurement.
How often self-proofreading misses errors

The best figures here come from a 1993 study by Daneman and Stainton. Raymond Panko, at the University of Hawaii, tabulates them on his error research page. Self-proofreading caught 81% of nonword errors and 59% of word errors after 20 minutes. After two weeks, those rates rose to 88% and 68%. Treat these as Panko's summary of that study, not as a fresh measurement.

Two patterns stand out. Nonword errors were caught more often than word errors at both time points. The second check, two weeks later, also scored higher than the first for both error types. The gap between error types is the one to plan around.

Panko also gives a wider range. He writes that people are 40% to 90% successful at finding an error when they work alone. That is a summary, not one measured rate, so do not plan around a single number. The point holds anyway. Expect to miss some errors in your own work.
Why real-word typos get past you

A nonword is easy to spot because it is not a word at all. 'Recieve' looks wrong on sight, and a spell checker flags it. A real-word error is harder. 'Affect' for 'effect,' 'site' for 'sight,' and 'their' for 'there' all look like words. They pass a spell checker, and they pass your eye. The word-error figures in the study sit lower than the nonword figures, which fits that pattern.

Doubled words such as 'the the' are another blind spot. Your eye jumps over the second copy, because it expects a new word there. Neither problem shows up well when you read for flow, so you need a separate check for each.
A worked example with a 10-error draft

Say your draft has 10 word errors. The 59% figure for word errors after 20 minutes suggests one self-pass catches about 6 of them. That leaves about 4 in the file. If you wait two weeks before the same check, the 68% figure suggests about 7 get caught. These numbers come from one older study, and your results will vary with the text and how closely you read.
Mistakes that make missed typos worse

items: Proofreading on the same screen, right after the last sentence you wrote.
Trusting one read because the draft looked clean the first time.
Treating the green and red underlines as the whole review.
Leaving names, numbers and headings for the last minute, then skipping them.
Switching to a hard-to-read font to force yourself to slow down.
Rereading only the parts you changed, and missing errors in the parts you did not.

blocks.text: When a second reader is worth it

BYU Editing Research recommends that someone else review important work before it goes out. Its examples include a dissertation, a job application and a self-published novel. For those, a second reader is worth the wait. A fresh reader sees what you have stopped seeing.

blocks.title: Client or patient data
blocks.text: If the draft holds client, patient, student or employer data, follow your employer's rules before you share it. That covers a friend, a proofreader or any AI tool, Lazur included. When in doubt, ask your manager first.
Which Mac checks catch what, and where they stop

Pages has a spelling and grammar checker built in. Word has Read Aloud, but Microsoft lists it only for Office 2019, Office 2021 and Microsoft 365 subscribers. Apple's Writing Tools can proofread selected text on a Mac with Apple Intelligence. Grammarly has a free plan and a Pro plan, which its site lists at $12 per month. blocks.text: Matching the check to the stakes

Match the check to the stakes. A newsletter can take one careful pass and a spelling check. A grant, a cover letter or a book chapter deserves a gap, a read aloud and a second reader if you can get one. Decide the plan before the final edit, not after you find the first error.

Keep a short list of the errors you repeat. Most writers have a few. If you always mix up 'lose' and 'loose,' put that pair on your list. In Pages, ⌃-click a name you keep spelling correctly and choose Learn Spelling. That teaches the spell checker the name. It does not fix a wrong word.

faq.question: Why do I miss typos in my own writing even after I reread it?
faq.answer: You read the meaning you intended, so your eyes fill in the correct word. Glynda Hull's 1987 study found that both more and less skilled college writers corrected very few errors in their own essays. Both groups did better on texts they did not write. Rereading the same draft tends to repeat the same blind spot.

faq.question: Does a spell checker catch every typo?
faq.answer: No. In the Daneman and Stainton figures, self-proofreading caught 81% of nonword errors and 59% of word errors after 20 minutes. Spell checkers flag words they do not recognize. Real words used in the wrong place, like 'their' for 'there,' need your own read or a second reader.

faq.question: Does reading aloud really help?
faq.answer: In Cushing and Bodner's 2022 study, reading aloud improved error detection compared with silent reading. The Learning Scientists post reports no percentages, so you cannot judge the size of the gain from that source alone. Reading aloud still costs nothing, so it is an easy test.

faq.question: How long should I wait before I proofread?
faq.answer: The 1993 figures rose after two weeks, so longer gaps appear to help. Most deadlines do not allow two weeks. Use the longest gap you have, even if it is only one night.

faq.question: Is Grammarly worth paying for?
faq.answer: Grammarly lists a Free plan at $0 per month and a Pro plan at $12 per month with a free trial. Its plans page does not show annual prices. It also does not confirm which plans include the Mac desktop app. Check their pricing page before you pay.

faq.question: Does Apple's Writing Tools Proofread work on my Mac?
faq.answer: Apple's page does not list a macOS version or hardware requirement for Proofread. It says Apple Intelligence is not available in all languages or regions, and usage limits may apply. Test it on a paragraph you know well before you rely on it.

faq.question: Can I paste a client's draft into an AI tool to proofread it?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your employer's rules still come first.

faq.question: Is a paid proofreader worth the money?
faq.answer: No source on this page gives proofreader prices, so there is no number to compare. BYU's editing team recommends another reader for important work, which can be a colleague or a friend. Start there before you pay for anything.

costs.title: Trust from the reader
costs.text: A reader who spots a typo may start to doubt the rest of the page. No study in these sources measures how often this happens. Treat it as a real risk, not a known rate. The reader pays this cost first, before you notice it.

costs.title: Rework after you send
costs.text: Once a file is out, fixes cost more. You may need a corrected version, a note to a client or a reissued PDF. No source here puts a time or money figure on that rework, so estimate it from your own past jobs.

costs.title: Thin income makes each miss sting
costs.text: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics counted about 140,300 writers and authors jobs in 2025. The median pay was $76,910 in May 2025, but that figure excludes self-employed workers. The Authors Guild's 2023 survey found a median full-time book income of $10,000 for 2022. If your income depends on a few contracts, one lost one hurts more.

costs.title: Time spent on double checks
costs.text: After one miss, it is tempting to reread everything again. That extra pass costs time you may not have planned. Time one full proof on your next draft, so you know your real number.

causes.title: You read the meaning, not the letters
causes.text: When you reread your own draft, your eyes follow the meaning you intended. The text on the page and the text in your head blur together. Hull's 1987 study points the same way. Both the more skilled and the less skilled writers struggled with their own essays. Carelessness is not the main issue here.

causes.title: Real words hide from your eye
causes.text: Misspelled nonwords stand out. Real-word errors like 'affect' for 'effect' look like correct words, so you skip them. In the 1993 figures, word errors were caught less often than nonword errors, at 59% against 81% after 20 minutes. A spell checker usually cannot tell which real word you meant.

causes.title: Silent reading lets your eyes slide
causes.text: In Cushing and Bodner's 2022 study, reading aloud improved error detection compared with silent reading. The Learning Scientists post reports that participants rated silent and aloud reading as equally effective. Yet they performed better aloud. Your gut says silent reading is fine. The test says otherwise.

causes.title: Time away from the draft seems to help
causes.text: The two-week figures in Panko's table are higher than the 20-minute figures for both error types. A draft you wrote this morning still feels fresh and correct. Based on those figures, distance seems to help you read it more like a stranger would. This is an inference from the numbers, not a tested rule.

causes.title: A hard font does not slow you down
causes.text: Some writers switch to a hard-to-read font, hoping it forces them to slow down. The Learning Scientists post reports that the disfluent Sans Forgetica font did not help. Difficulty alone is not a fix. Pick a plain font you read easily and check the words themselves.

fixes.title: Read it aloud, one paragraph at a time
fixes.text: Reading aloud beat silent reading for catching errors in Cushing and Bodner's 2022 study, according to The Learning Scientists. Word for Mac has Read Aloud on the Review tab. Start it with ⌃⌥Space, play or pause with ⌥Space, and move between paragraphs with ⌥↑ or ⌥↓. If you do not have Read Aloud, read the draft out loud yourself, slowly, one paragraph at a time.

fixes.title: Run Pages' spelling and grammar check
fixes.text: In Pages, choose Edit > Spelling and Grammar > Check Grammar With Spelling. Then choose Edit > Spelling and Grammar > Check Document Now. Grammar problems show as green underlines. Press ⌘; to jump to the next misspelled word. Use ⌃-click > Learn Spelling for a name you use often, since macOS shares that word with other apps.

fixes.title: Ask Writing Tools to proofread
fixes.text: Select the paragraph you want checked, then ⌃-click it. Choose Writing Tools > Show Writing Tools, click Proofread, and click Done when you finish. Apple's page says Apple Intelligence may not be available in your language or region. Test it on a paragraph you know well before you rely on it.

fixes.title: Leave a gap before the final check
fixes.text: The Daneman and Stainton figures rose after two weeks. Word errors went from 59% to 68%, and nonword errors went from 81% to 88%. Most deadlines do not allow two weeks. Use the longest gap you have, even if it is only one night.

fixes.title: Search for the pairs you mix up
fixes.text: Write down the word pairs you confuse, such as its and it's, to and too, and affect and effect. In Pages or Word, press ⌘F, search each pair, and read every hit in its sentence. Search for doubled words such as 'the the' the same way. Fix only what is wrong.

fixes.title: Ask for a second read the right way
fixes.text: Name the error types you want checked, such as typos, names and numbers. Give a deadline and send a clean copy with no tracked changes. A focused request gets a more useful read than 'Can you look at this?'

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Finish the draft and stop
plan.text: Write until the draft is done. Do not edit as you go. Write down the three word pairs you mix up most, and keep the list in your notes app.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Run the spelling pass
plan.text: Open the draft in Pages. Choose Edit > Spelling and Grammar > Check Grammar With Spelling, then Check Document Now. Press ⌘; to step through each flag. Fix real errors only.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Leave the file alone
plan.text: Do not open the file. If your deadline allows, leave it for at least a night. The 1993 figures rose after two weeks, so longer is better when you can. Set a reminder in Apple Reminders for when you return.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Search for the pairs
plan.text: Press ⌘F, search each word pair from Day 1, and read every hit in its sentence. Search for doubled words such as 'the the.' Fix what is wrong and leave the rest.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Read it aloud
plan.text: Use Word's Read Aloud if you have it, or read the draft yourself in full sentences. Pause at commas and stop at any line that sounds off. Mark it, then keep going.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Get a second read
plan.text: Send the draft to a second reader with a clear request: check typos, names and numbers. If the draft holds client or patient data, check your employer's rules before you share it with anyone.
